catalog_quote: First, all lexical words have lexical prominence or primary stress (‘obligatoriness parameter’) with one syllable bearing the highest degree of prominence – ‘culminativity parameter’ (Hyman 2006). Second, stressed vowels are longer than unstressed vowels. As previously mentioned, glottalized vowels always occur under stress and are double the duration of modal vowels, hence my analysis of them as bimoraic. In terms of metrical structure, I propose that (i) the Nivaĉle foot type is iambic, and (ii) the Nivaĉle language has a quantity-sensitive stress system, where the moraic weight of the feature [constricted glottis] is consistently correlated with stress prominence. Stress assignment in the nominal domain varies across the alienable vs. inalienable paradigm. In alienable nouns, primary stress is final. sweep_summary: Both works with stress in the title are by Analía Gutiérrez and were obtained and read. (1) The 2015 UBC dissertation (already listed; UBC's live host blocks our network, but a 22 MB Internet Archive copy of the cIRcle PDF was downloaded) contains the full stress analysis (ch. 4, pp. 153-213): quantity-sensitive iambic system, moraic /ʔ/, final stress in disyllabic roots, primary stress on the rightmost foot of the Prosodic Word, morphological-edge alignment; it confirms the catalog's classification and is the primary behind the JIPA deciding quote. (2) The 2016 LIAMES glottal-stop paper (open access, not previously listed) is about the prosodic parsing of /ʔ/; its only stress content is the Weight-to-Stress licensing of glottalized vowels and a footnote summarizing the dissertation, so it confirms but adds nothing. Bonus: Stell's 1987 UBA doctoral grammar (the source behind the surveys' transmitted alternating row, cited 'Stell 1989' by Gutiérrez) is openly available at repositorio.filo.uba.ar and was downloaded (2 vols., scanned text layer, page images of pp. 81-83 checked): primary stress is root-final 'con una frecuencia mayor', shifted by suffixes; secondary stress on the 2nd and 4th syllable from the left in 4+ syllable words, with no weight statement. That closes most of the editor note's 'Stell pin': the survey's 'odd-numbered from R' alternation is not what Stell describes (she counts from the left, hedged), and Gutiérrez rejects her secondary-stress data. Stell 1972 (Fonología de la lengua Axluxlaj) remains unlocated online. No change to the catalog's classification is indicated; the dissertation and Stell 1987 should be added as corroborating/refining sources. and.

new_statements.quote: In this section, I consider the different word-stress patterns in Nivaĉle and propose that (i) the foot type is iambic, and (ii) the Nivaĉle language has a quantity-sensitive stress system, where the moraic weight of /ʔ/ is consistently correlated with stress prominence, and (iii) a CVC syllable in word initial position – and only in this position of convergent morphological and prosodic prominence – is stressed [...] Main stress falls on the rightmost foot of the Prosodic Word. [...] Turning our attention to disyllabic roots, the basic generalization is that stress is final, motivating the claim that the stress system of Nivaĉle is right-headed, or iambic.

new_statements.reading: Word-level, culminative primary stress assigned by quantity-sensitive iambic footing: only vowels and the postvocalic glottal stop are moraic (coda consonants are not), glottalized/glottal-coda syllables are heavy and always stressed, disyllabic roots are otherwise final-stressed, primary stress sits on the rightmost foot of the Prosodic Word, foot parsing is aligned to morphological edges (root/stem/word right edge; possessive-prefix left edge), and an initial CVC can take secondary stress. Rightward-alternating secondaries are not described; the alternation in the surveys traces to Stell 1987:83 (2nd and 4th syllable from the left), which Gutiérrez disputes (pp. 156-158). This is the same author's fuller primary analysis of what the catalog's deciding JIPA statement condenses; it supports the weight-conditioned (weight-hedged / weight-sensitive) coding and adds the explicit rightmost-foot rule.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding JIPA quotation is verbatim in the extracted text we hold at p. 413 'Stress' section, exactly where the locator says; the Cuadernos 2019 and Fabre 2016 corroborating passages are also present in copies we hold. (2) Deciding source: a JIPA Illustration (2016 online / 2019 print) with instrumental duration data, written by the author of the 2015 UBC phonology dissertation on this language; corroborated by the held 542-pp Fabre 2016 grammar (final stress 'generalmente', non-distinctive, glottalized /ɒ̰/ attracts stress) — all consistent with the catalog's right-edge iambic, weight(=glottalization)-sensitive, 'weight-hedged' coding. Two further open Gutiérrez papers downloaded now (WCCFL 33 2016 pp. 183-184; CJL 2020 p. 282) restate the same analysis and add the morphological edge-alignment detail (prefixed MSt2 forms align left, giving penult stress in ji-k͡lé.sa, ji-ʃín.βo)

sources.quote: 'Finally, Nivaĉle has a quantity-sensitive iambic stress system. There is a consistent correlation between bimoraic weight (tautosyllabic /Vʔ/) and stress prominence. In addition, primary/secondary stress patterns reflect competing edge-alignment constraints where prosodic foot domains align with internal morphological category (MCat) edges, specifically Root (Rt), Stem1 (St1), Stem2 (StressTyp2), and Morphological Word (MWd). For a fuller explanation of Nivaĉle stress assignment domains, see Gutiérrez (2015).'

sources.citation: Gutiérrez, Analía. 2016. The variable prosodic parsings of Nivaĉle glottal stop. LIAMES: Línguas Indígenas Americanas 16(2): 323-347. (Glottolog 662304; DOI 10.20396/liames.v16i2.8646180; not previously listed)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: given that there is a consistent correlation between glottalized vowels and the locus of stress, I propose that a postvocalic glottal stop is, like vowels, underlyingly moraic. Recall that the Weight-to-Stress Principle (Prince & Smolensky 1993) states that heavy (bimoraic) syllables are required to be stressed. (p. 18) [...] A superficially complex stress system in Nivaĉle is shown to reduce to systematic regularities of three types. First, it is shown that stress is quantity-sensitive, with a consistent correlation between bimoraic weight (tautosyllabic /Vʔ/) and stress prominence. Secondly, primary/secondary stress patterns reflect competing edge-alignment constraints where prosodic foot domains align with internal morphological category (MCat) edges. (fn. 6, p. 24)
sources.locator: PDF p. 18 (§ on /Vʔ/ representation) and footnote 6, PDF p. 24 (journal pagination 323-347)
sources.note: Paper is about the featural and prosodic parsing of the glottal stop (onset vs. complex nucleus vs. coda), not stress placement; stress appears only as the licensing condition for glottalized vowels (moraic /ʔ/, Weight-to-Stress) and in a footnote that summarizes the dissertation's three-part stress analysis and defers to Gutiérrez (2015). No new placement rule or examples of stress location beyond the dissertation.

sources.quote: a) El acento primario cae en la raíz y en determinados afijos de flexión y de derivación. Cuando las raíces son bisílabas o trisílabas el acento primario cae, con una frecuencia mayor, estadísticamente comprobada, en la última sílaba. En las construcciones morfológicas constituidas por raíces monosílabas y bisílabas la presencia de determinados sufijos de flexión y de derivación desplazan regularmente el acento primario a la última sílaba. En las construcciones morfológicas de cuatro o más sílabas el acento primario se mantiene, en general, en la raíz [...] (p. 81) b) El acento secundario cae en la segunda y cuarta sílaba de construcciones morfológicas de cuatro o más sílabas, siempre que no coincida con el acento primario (p. 83) — Translation: a) Primary stress falls on the root and on certain inflectional and derivational affixes. When roots are disyllabic or trisyllabic, primary stress falls, with a statistically verified higher frequency, on the last syllable. In morphological constructions made of monosyllabic and disyllabic roots, certain inflectional and derivational suffixes regularly shift primary stress to the last syllable. sources.note: The earliest first-hand description (Axluxlaj/Alhulhai speakers, fieldwork 1971) and the only primary source behind the surveys' transmitted row (StressTyp2 i2@1R / Gordon 'Odd-numbered from R', which the editor note attributed to unread Stell 1972). Primary stress: root-final 'with a higher frequency', hedged ('en general', 'con una frecuencia mayor'), morphologically shifted by suffixes; secondary stress on the 2nd and 4th syllables counted from the LEFT in words of 4+ syllables, with a stated ban on more than two consecutive unstressed syllables; examples 'is / i'sis, k'a'sus / k'asu'sik,…
